en: [II,1 Hiraṇya’s Experiences] In the southern country there was a city named Mithilāropya;
not far from it was a dwelling for wandering mendicants.
There lived a wandering mendicant named Jūṭakarṇa.
At the time for alms, he went from that city to the houses of the brahmins, being regarded as a holy site (*tīrtha*), [receiving] portions of sugar-candy and pomegranate seeds.
Having filled his alms-bowl with various kinds of food that were smooth, liquid, and delicate,
he returned to that dwelling; having performed the ritual observance for the time of the vow according to the rules,
he placed the remainder there in a well-secured container on a peg.
I live with my retinue by means of that [food].
Even though it is very carefully placed there, as it is being consumed in this way, he becomes weary of it and,
out of fear of me, moves it from one place to another higher up.
"I obtain that too without effort and eat it.
Now, as time passed in this manner, once a guest named Bṛhatsphig arrived at his place as a wandering mendicant.
Having performed the hospitable reception for him and completed the appropriate time for his religious observances, Jūṭakarṇa concealed the remainder of that āpūtaka in a well-hidden place within it;
then, sitting on his couch, he questioned Bṛhatsphija, who was lying on the bed.
"Since you were separated from me here,
in which other lands or penance groves have you wandered since then?
He replied:
Then once, on the great full moon day of Kārttika, having performed my ablutions at Puṣkara, the most excellent of great tīrthas, I was separated from you due to the fault of a vast crowd of people.
Thereafter, I [visited] Gaṅgādvāra, Prayāga, Vārāṇasī, and other such places.
Wandering along the Ganges, both with and against the current,
why say more? He beheld the entire circle of the earth, bounded by the ocean.
While that was only half-told, the wandering mendicant Jūṭakarṇa, leaning against a wooden pillar, repeatedly played a worn-out lute.
And when the narration was thus interrupted, Bṛhatsphig became angry and said:
Having become respectful, I speak to you;
but for what reason are you disrespectful?
And likewise:
"Disrespect, recounting misdeeds, engaging in idle talk, and lack of awe toward speech."
"Not bestowing one's vision nor destroying what has been done is the characteristic of a man whose nature is dispassionate.
He said:
"My good man, you should not be angry.
Look: this mouse of mine does great harm;
it destroys my alms-bowl, and yet I am unable to ward it off."
He said:
"Is this the only mouse here, or are there other mice as well?"
He said:
"What is the use of other mice?
This wicked one deceives me constantly, like a sorcerer."
Having heard that, he said:
"Jūṭakarṇa, a mere mouse does not possess such power. What, then, must be the cause here?"
And it has been said:
"Śāṇḍilī’s mother does not sell sesame for sesame without a reason; she exchanges the husked for the unhusked—there must be some purpose behind this. (45)
Jūṭakarṇa said,
"How was that? He replied:
[II,2 Hulled Sesame for Hulled] It happened that once, during the approaching rainy season, I requested a certain brahmin for lodging in a particular settlement in order to take up residence there.
When the rains had passed, having awakened during the final watch of the night for the sake of returning to the monastery, I thought:
"By which direction should I proceed?"
Then, at that very moment, the brahmin also woke up and asked his wife, who was behind the lattice:
"O Brahmani, listen!"
"Tomorrow will be a festival day;
on that occasion, you must provide a meal for the brahmins according to your ability.
He replied with words of many harsh syllables:
"How can you, who are utterly destitute, have the means for feeding brahmins?
When he was addressed thus, he remained as if cast into a well and did not say a word.
After a long time, he spoke again.
O Brāhmaṇī, one should always practice accumulation, but one should not practice excessive accumulation; for this jackal, being habituated to excessive accumulation, was killed by a bow. (46)
He said:
"And how is this so?
The Brahmin replied.
[II,3 The Overly Greedy Jackal] In a certain place there was a hunter who subsisted on meat. Having risen at dawn and entered a certain forest, he quickly [saw] a deer.
Having pierced [the boar] and accumulated a mass of flesh, as he was returning and descending at a great bathing place,
he saw a boar resembling a young buffalo, with its tusks uprooted and its body smeared with lumps of mud.
Seeing him, he was overcome with fear, prompted by the sight of that inauspicious omen;
turning back, his movement obstructed, the boar contracted the meat,
threw it upon the ground, fixed an arrow to his bow, and spoke as follows:
"I have neither my bow nor even my arrows strung; why does this boar approach with such suspicion?
I shall see his true intent by force."
"Surely this has been sent to me by Yama!"—
having said this, he discharged a poison-smeared arrow at him; having pierced him at the joint of the neck, he caused it to pass through to the other side.
Even the boar, though stunned by the blow, exerted his utmost speed and struck him so violently in the refuse heap that he lost his life.

The body of the one who had gone [to heaven] fell in three parts. Then, when that great and terrible slaughter of deer, hunters, and boars had occurred, a peacock named Darduraka, his belly emaciated by hunger and seeking food, went to that place.
Having arrived, he saw the deer, the boar, and the hunter;
and seeing them, he attained the highest satisfaction and said:
"Indeed, food and drink constantly arise for embodied beings;
having obtained abundant food and provisions, one should consume them gradually.
(48) Thus it is said.
Having spoken thus, he began to chew through the fastening of the bow;
somehow, by fate, when the fastening was severed, his chest was pierced and he passed away. [2,2]
Therefore I say:
"One must always make an accumulation.
That is so, O Brāhmaṇī.
"Life is sustained by clarity.
Having heard this, the Brahmin woman said,
"I have a small amount of sesame and a small amount of rice."
Therefore, rise at dawn and go to the forest to fetch fuel, *kuśa* grass, and other necessities;
I too, along with this disciple Kāmandaki, [shall attend] to the three Brahmins.
"I shall prepare the *kṛsara*," he said.
When it was thus carried out, he ordered that a *prastha* of sesame seeds be plucked while Kāmandakī stood over them.
And so, because he was extremely preoccupied, those sesame seeds somehow became defiled with excrement by a dog;
she, remaining inside, saw this, and then she said:
Kāmandakī: Something unfortunate has occurred; an obstacle has arisen to the Brahmins' gratification.
Nevertheless, go.
"Even though these sesame seeds have been husked, exchange them for black sesame seeds and return quickly;
I shall prepare only black *kṛsara*."
When it had been carried out accordingly, at the very house where I had arrived for alms,
Kāmandaki also entered for the purpose of selling sesame seeds and said,
"Let these sesame seeds be taken."
The Brahmin woman asked,
"How are the sesame seeds to be given?
Kāmandaki replied:
"I give you white ones in exchange for black ones; take whatever you desire.
"In that case, O blessed lady, since these have been plucked out, give me only those that have been plucked out.
When this had been done, her husband arrived.
He said to her,
"My dear lady, what is this?
She replied to him:
"I have obtained sesame seeds of equal value—
white ones for black ones.
Thereupon, he laughed and said:
"It is not without cause that the mother Śāṇḍilī exchanges sesame seeds for sesame seeds;
she exchanges only those that have been husked for those that have been husked. There must be a reason for this.
(50) Thus it was said.
Having spoken thus, the wandering mendicant said,
"Is there any digging tool?
Jūṭakarṇa replied:
"Certainly; it exists.
When he had been brought forward, [the king] tightened his girdle, bit his lips, and asked:
"Which is his path of passage?"
When that had been said, he began to perform the rite of digging;
and I, having heard their private conversation from the very beginning, cast aside my food and remained there,
intent on curiosity.
But when he began to search for a difficult passage,
I realized that this wicked-souled one had discovered the entrance to my burrow.
"I too had previously obtained some gold deposited by a certain virtuous man;
because of that, I considered myself powerful.
That wicked man, however, having discovered it by following the trail of the hole and having seized the wealth, [returned] again—"
Having reached that state, he said to Jūṭakarṇa:
"This is that Brahmahṛdaya,
by the power of which even the impossible becomes possible."
He rose up from his place,
and having divided [the seat] into two halves, they remained seated comfortably.
Then, experiencing this dejection of my own, I reflected:
"Perhaps while I am staying here, they might light a lamp and, having found me without a doubt, kill me.
Thinking thus, he made for himself another stronghold from that place.
And others as well, who were my followers, came and said to me:
"O auspicious Hiraṇya!"
We, who are staying near you, are extremely tormented by hunger; we do not have even a single morsel of food. Even though the day has set, nothing has been obtained by us.
"Therefore, you ought to satisfy us even now.

Having said, "So be it," I went with them to their dwelling. Standing in a secluded spot, I listened to the remainder of the conversation between those two evil-minded men, which had been previously mentioned.
I heard that Jūṭakarṇa was likewise shaking his lineage during the narration. He was addressed by him [the king]:
Why do you still keep moving the flute again and again even though it has been discarded?
Please stop; enough!
Since he said,
"Good sir, this mouse who does me harm comes again and again," the other laughed and replied:
Do not fear;
this is nothing at all. For:
"One becomes powerful through wealth; from wealth one becomes wise.
Behold this wicked mouse, who has attained a state equal to his own kind! (51) Moreover:
"That which is the cause of its power to fly is already in our hands; however,
I have already secured it in that very manner."
"This man speaks the truth;
even I, Aṅgulimāla, have no power to leap up today," he thought,
as he heard the conversation of his followers among themselves.
"Come, let us go;
he is not capable even of bending a blade of grass today.
Having said this, about fifty of them departed.
Again there are twenty-five; ten and five. Then others are twelve and eight;
then the remaining two.
Thereupon, one of them said:
"This man is not even capable of filling his own belly, much less those of others."
Having said this, he departed without further concern;
then, reflecting thus, I went to my own abode.
At the time of dawn, all of us indeed went into the presence of our rival.
Saying, "This man is poor," not even a single one of his followers who were engaged in that manner came into my presence.
And I saw that, upon seeing me face to face,
my attendants were playing together with my rivals, shouting "kilakila" and clapping their hands.
And I thought:
"It is even so;
he who has wealth has friends; he who has wealth has kinsmen."
He who possesses wealth is a man in this world; he who possesses wealth is a wise scholar.
Furthermore:
For a man of small intellect who is bereft of wealth...
All activities are cut short, like the water in a small stream during the summer.
Friends, sons, wives, and well-wishers abandon one who is destitute of wealth; yet they resort once again to that same person when he possesses riches.
For in this world, wealth is indeed a person's kinsman. // 54 //
No one accepts the words of a poor man, even if he is wise and speaks sweetly, when they are spoken at the proper time.
The outcaste and the pauper—these two are considered equal;
for the outcaste does not receive, and the pauper does not give.
But when a man is deprived of wealth and has become untouchable,
all his kinsmen abandon him, just as the vital breaths leave a dead being.
A man devoid of wealth is abandoned by friends and kinsmen; having lost his worldly activities and his wife, he is like one whose life has departed, shorn of all luster. (58)
The house of one without a son is empty; he who has no true friend is long empty;
the directions are empty for the fool; everything is empty for the poor man.
"Arise for a single moment, my friend! Bear this heavy burden of poverty while I, being weary, enjoy for a long time the bliss of death.
Thus addressed by a learned man destitute of wealth, a corpse went to the cremation ground.
"Having realized that death is better than poverty because it brings happiness, he remained silent.
What else, sirs?
No one else even gave a reply."
Those very same senses are unimpaired, that very same name remains, that very same intellect is unobstructed, and that very same speech persists;
yet it is that same man who is now bereft of the warmth of wealth.
He lies with all his limbs contracted like the letter *ha*.
Such is generally the nature of people in this world;
even upon seeing a noble person who has fallen into misfortune, one becomes deaf, blind, and mute.
Due to the arrogance born of the intoxication of wealth;
and likewise:
"He gazes with unimpaired eyes."
His speech is clear and free from corruption; alas, such cruelty has been exercised by these riches that the Lord has been reduced to the state of a petitioner! [62]
Therefore, what indeed would be a boon for those like me,
who would have such a ripening of fruit?
That he constantly says "Give," is in every way not for my benefit here now that I am destitute of wealth.
And it is said:

"One should not dwell in a place where one's honor is diminished, nor should one associate with those whose honor is low; one should avoid even a celestial palace if it is shared with those of little honor.
Having spoken thus, I nevertheless reflected once more in this way:
For what purpose shall I make myself a petitioner to anyone? That indeed is more painful;
and for what reason?
Better is the birth of even a hunchbacked tree, gnawed by insects, its bark stripped away by forest fires, and standing in barren soil, than that of one who is a petitioner.
Hoarseness in the throat, perspiration on the face, discoloration, and trembling—
these very signs that belong to one who is dying are also present in one who begs; thus,
even such begging is base.
It robs the intellect of its dispassion, it is the abode of false conceptualizations,
a synonym for death, a dwelling place of wretchedness, and the supreme repository of doubt. It is embodied insignificance, the seat of calamities, and the thief of the splendor of the proud.
For I see no other thing for the high-minded than hell resulting from their state of supplication.
Moreover:
"One who lacks wealth falls into shame; one overcome by shame falls away from his splendor."
One who lacks splendor is despised; from being despised, one falls into despondency. Despondent, one succumbs to grief; with a grieving mind, one's intellect perishes.
Devoid of intellect, one goes to ruin—alas, the state of death is the abode of all calamities!
Moreover:
It would be better to place both hands in the mouth of a serpent filled with rage;
it would be better to drink poison and fall asleep in the abode of Yama.
It would be better for one's self to be cast from the slope of the best of mountains and shatter into a hundred pieces,
than to achieve one's own pleasure through wealth obtained from wicked people.
"It is better that one who is destitute of wealth should satisfy the fire with his own life than that he should entreat a miserable person who has fallen away from proper conduct.
Now, since things have come to this pass, by what means might there be life?
And what of theft?
Even that taking of another's property is more grievous,
for this reason:
Silence is better than speaking words that are false;
death is more praiseworthy than approaching the wife of another;
the abandonment of life is better than delighting in the speech of the malicious.
It is better to seek alms than to repeatedly taste the wealth of others.
For even when a man seeks such things, contempt is certain;
how so?
[But the reversal of one's disposition is a humiliation of the intellect; it is like the loss of hope for one who seeks, or like another form of death.
Now, why should I sustain myself with the alms of others?
Alas!
That too is the second gateway to death:
"The sick man, the long-traveler, the one who eats another's food, and the one who sleeps in another's dwelling."
That which is living is itself death; that is his rest.
Furthermore:
Born into a great family, he was arrogant, intoxicated by the wealth of honor.
Rejoicing as if at a time of honor and prosperity, he eats even that leftover morsel of the king; what could be more miserable than this, like a dog? (73)
For one whose mind is overwhelmed by hope, non-attainment is better than the attainment of what is desired, for through non-attainment, longing becomes attenuated;
whereas the joy arising from the acquisition of what is wished for is all the more destructive to steadfastness.
Like the breaking of a dam by waters, helplessness is spread abroad by its force.
Moreover:
[Of those who cast their eyes askance with smiles, raising one eyebrow on high...]
Having heard the harsh words of the wealthy, whose heads are held high with arrogance,
why does the chest of those supplicants who serve them not burst asunder immediately?
It would, were it not for the fact that their inner core is so firmly solidified by the iron-strength of craving.

If our wife is seen with her wretched face, her tattered clothes pulled by her own piteous children who cry out in hunger, while the food-vessels are empty and she utters but half-syllables with a throat faltering from the fear of a rejected plea; ||| ...then what is the use of wealth? (The verse continues: Even if one possesses a hundred jars of gold, if one does not give even a small portion to a beggar who has come seeking, that wealth is like a treasure hidden in the earth—it is of no use to the man himself. ||| Therefore, O King, give this wealth to the poor, for it is through giving that wealth becomes truly meaningful. It is better to give even a little than to possess much that is not given. ||| For when one departs from this world, neither father nor mother follows behind; only the merit earned through charity follows the departing soul. ||| Thus, O King, practice generosity toward the poor, for it is the giver who attains happiness in both this world and the next. ||| And so it is said: "Better is a small gift given at the right time than a great amount given at the wrong time; a gift given at the proper moment brings great fruit. ||| Therefore, O King, give this wealth to the poor, for it is through giving that wealth becomes truly meaningful. It is better to give even a little than to possess much that is not given. ||| For when one departs from this world, neither father nor mother follows behind; only the merit earned through charity follows the departing soul. ||| Thus, O King, practice generosity toward the poor, for it is the giver who attains happiness in both this world and the next. ||| And so it is said: "Better is a small gift given at the right time than a great amount given at the wrong time; a gift given at the proper moment brings great fruit. ||| Therefore, O King, give this wealth to the poor, for it is through giving that wealth becomes truly meaningful. It is better to give even a little than to possess much that is not given. ||| For when one departs from this world, neither father nor mother follows behind; only the merit earned through charity follows the departing soul. ||| Thus, O King, practice generosity toward the poor, for it is the giver who attains happiness in both this world and the next. ||| And so it is said: "Better is a small gift given at the right time than a great amount given at the wrong time; a gift given at the proper moment brings great fruit. ||| Therefore, O King, give this wealth to the poor, for it is through giving that wealth becomes truly meaningful. What wise man would say "Give! for the sake of his own scorched belly?
Thus, this poverty is a form of death in many ways.
Now, if I were to make that very wealth my own—
"But I, having previously seen those dinars, made them my pillow for those two wicked men and concealed them;
having reflected thus, I went to that place."
Then, thinking that they were distracted, I approached them with the desire to seize them;
but seeing me, Bṛhatsphik struck me with a club.
I too, wishing for death, somehow retreated.
Once again, after a long time, having regained hope and comforted himself, he approached the dinar;
by that same merciless man, he was struck on the head in such a way that even today, it remains as if it were in a dream.
I am terrified of such people. Look at this wound on my head, inflicted by him at that time.
And it is well said:
Having encountered a perilous calamity that threatens the destruction of all his life-breaths,
one whose fear is imminent does not perceive his own life as distressed, yet he longs for it;
but once he has emerged from that, for the sake of wealth, he enters yet another calamity.
The stake is the mutual cause of both life and wealth for those whose minds are intent on acquisition.
Having reflected deeply, I have desisted from craving, thinking, "This wealth is mine."
And this is well said:
"Knowledge is the eye; it is not mere morality, nor noble lineage, nor birth into a good family.
Contentment is true prosperity, and wisdom is the unimpeded cessation [of defilements]. (78)
All prosperity belongs to him whose mind is content;
for one whose feet are covered by shoes, the entire earth is as if covered with leather.
For one driven by craving, even a hundred yojanas is not too far;
for one who is content, there is no regard even for an object already in hand. (80)
Snakes drink only air yet they do not become weak;
forest elephants grow strong on leaves and grass;
and the best of sages pass their time on roots and fruits.
Contentment alone is the supreme wealth of the great.
Therefore, in every respect, it is better to exercise restraint regarding an object that cannot be attained;
begging is the ultimate form of poverty, not the mere paucity of riches.
"Śambhu possesses wealth in the form of an old bull, yet he is still the Supreme Lord.
And likewise:
"What is dharma? Compassion for living beings. What is happiness for a creature? Freedom from disease."
What is affection? It is the state of being real. What is wisdom? It is discernment. // 83 //
"There are vegetables in the forests and rivers with pure water;
the moon is this common lamp—what is the use of riches?
(84) Thus it is said.
Having resolved this, I returned to my own abode and saw Citragrīva bound by a snare;
and having liberated him with the help of this Laghupatanaka, I have come into your presence.
[The story of the poor Somilaka:
There was a certain town where a weaver named Somilaka used to live.
Whatever he earned did not exceed his daily expenses;
becoming weary of this, he departed for another land.
There, with great hardship, he earned one hundred dīnāras within three years;
then he set out for his own country.
When he had reached the middle of the road at the time of twilight, he arrived at the foot of a banyan tree in the midst of a forest.
He reached [the village] and thought: "Where shall I go now, for the village is very far away?"
"Therefore, I shall spend the night having climbed this very banyan tree.
Having thus resolved, he did so.
And at midnight, he saw two men, as if in a dream.
Two beings of immense size and divine form, their eyes bloodshot with rage, approached his presence;
one of them spoke.
O Vaṅkālaka!
So it is;
you have already been warned by me many times before.
"Just as nothing other than food and drink should be given to this Somilaka,
so too a hundred dinars are due to him today."
"Take it away quickly!
Then he replied,
"As you command, O Lord."
"I shall do so.
Having heard this, he woke up and looked around,
but did not see the hundred dīnāras.
With a dejected heart, he thought: "Alas!
What is this?"
"How have I been deceived here by some being?
What shall I do now after going home?
Having turned back from here, once I have acquired wealth again, I shall go."
Reflecting thus, when the night had turned to dawn, he reached the city once more;
setting his mind upon acquiring wealth, after some time he earned fifty dinars and set out again on that same path to return to his own country.
Impelled by destiny, one does not obtain anything more than that,
nor does one go by another path;
one is led to that very place.
When the sun had set, he reached that very banyan tree and thought to himself:
"Alas!
What is this that has been undertaken by this wretched fate?
That very same Rākṣasa, in the form of a banyan tree, has fallen upon us once again!"
Thinking thus, as he was falling asleep, he saw these two men. One of them said:
"O Vaṅkāla!"
"Fifty dinars belong to Somilaka;
that is not right.
Thereupon, he said:
"Understand that they have been carried off.
But Somilaka, having woken up, did not see them carried off. Then, filled with despondency, he said:
"What use have I for life?
What is this occurrence,
and by what cause has my wealth been acquired through affliction?"
"I do not know who is carrying me away; now I shall give up my life. Thinking thus, he remained right there without food.
After only a few days,
he saw a man of divine appearance,
who said to him:
"O Somilaka!
I am Dhanada.
I do not bestow wealth upon anyone who is unworthy."
And thus:
"That which was not to be will not be; that which is to be will not be otherwise.
Why is this medicine, which destroys the poison of anxiety, not drunk? (113)
While lying down, one person unexpectedly attains fruit; another, despite having exerted effort, perishes;
and people merely dance about due to their lack of self-restraint.
But as for the ritual procedure, wherever one desires it, there success is attained.
Neither physical form bears fruit, nor virtues, nor heroism; neither learning, nor even excellence produced through effort.
It is destiny alone, accumulated from the store of the fruits of past actions, that brings results.
In due time, they bear fruit for a person, just like trees. // 115 //
Even when angry, who can cause suffering to another?
And who, even when joyful, can bestow happiness upon another?
For the world is bound by the knots of its own karma.
The conceit that "the agent acts" is in vain. // 116 //
"Intelligent, highly energetic, wise, brave, and of noble birth—
endowed with hands and feet, yet they have fallen into the service of others.
What is the use of lamenting over this, Somilaka?"
Apart from food and drink, you have no means of acquiring wealth whatsoever.
Others carry the palanquin, while others have already mounted it; eloquence is indeed causeless, and old age is merely a state of being cast out. (118)
A living being does not necessarily obtain [their goal] through the power of mantras, through vigor, through wisdom, or through human effort; what cause for lamentation is there in this? (119)
One obtains only what is to be obtained; one goes only where it is to be gone; and one experiences only those sufferings and joys that are to be experienced. (120)
Just as misfortunes come upon embodied beings unbidden, I believe that joys likewise do; in this matter, fate prevails.
Who distinguishes another, by what means is one made superior, or who is born with wealth? Who is poor?
Fortunes are as steady or as fickle as bees.
[They] constantly wander among human flowers.
Nevertheless, the production of wealth results from the conjunction of destiny and human effort; the person acts, and destiny [responds].
"It bears fruit.
To this, you, intent on your exertion, replied: "I have been seen by you;
my sight is not in vain."
"What indeed shall I do for you? He replied, "Give me wealth."
Dhanada laughed and said, "Fool! What indeed is done with this? Enjoyment is the purpose here."
"Go! In this very city, look for two merchants:
one wealthy and the other possessing great enjoyments. Having seen them, observe what each of them desires."
"You shall become such," he said, and then vanished.
At dawn, Somilaka also entered that city and approached the caravan leader.
He reached Dhanagupta;
there, although being rebuked, he somehow entered the house and remained sitting on the porch.
That merchant also, having passed the twilight, took a small amount of food at the onset of night;
he likewise had Somilaka take a small amount of food.
Then that weaver, having spread out kusha grass on the ground, fell asleep and saw those same two men;
one of them said:
"O Vaṅkāla! Today,
